text:
TV’s Natalie Pike: I turned detective to catch my stalker
“Long before Manchester City became a club besieged, Natalie Pike established herself as a face of its watershed moments, hosting the club’s homecoming parade from Istanbul after winning the Treble and conducting a poignant last interview with Pep Guardiola as he signed off his decade in charge. The Etihad Stadium was so comfortingly familiar that it became her sanctuary. That was until February 21 this year, when, in the midst of presenting pitchside during City’s 2-1 win over Newcastle, she grew conscious of a man hovering uncomfortably close to the barriers, intent on spooking her. “I just had a sense that something wasn’t right,” she says. “So I looked over my shoulder, and I instantly saw him – the man from the picture.”
 This picture was one she had excavated from Instagram, in a burst of panic about a traumatic episode eight days earlier. On that occasion, Pike, emerging from a restful spa day with a friend, had turned on her telephone to see a spate of missed calls from her hairdresser and the school attended by her eight-year-old son, Reggie. Two men, it turned out, had pulled up outside the salon in a van, telling staff that they knew Pike was a customer and demanding to know where she lived. The hairdresser alerted the school, conscious that it was on the same village road. “My friend said that I just went white,” she reflects. “I had no idea what it could mean. So I did what we tend to do as women, and I started investigating myself.”
 As a former model and now a versatile football presenter across BBC Sport, TNT Sports and CBS in the United States, the 43-year-old has built a substantial online presence. And when she trawled through previously hidden Instagram messages from people she did not follow, she noticed a high number across 18 months from one particular account. “They began in the usual way: ‘Happy birthday’, ‘You’re beautiful’, that kind of thing. Then they started deteriorating. So I took a screenshot of this person’s profile, sent it to my hairdresser, and she instantly confirmed it was the same man she had seen.” It would also be the same man who so unsettled her at City, although by the time she had a clear view he was bounding up the stairs to the concourse, desperate to avoid detection.
 Despite her increased prominence on television, Pike had never entertained the idea she could be the victim of stalking. She had also never intended to discuss the ordeal openly. “Whenever I’m on screen, you’ll see me very bubbly, smiley, happy,” she says. “But I’m also a very private person. My family and friends have encouraged me to do this, because I almost don’t want to admit that these things are real.” 
 Amid her maelstrom of emotions at the Etihad, she faced the same conundrum. Was there a possibility of mistaken identity? After the scare at the salon, she had contacted police, who duly tracked down the man she had discovered on social media and warned him to stay away from her. Or did she trust her instincts and decide that it was the same tormentor?
 “I ran up to the public address announcer’s room, and I had my first experience of a panic attack,” she says. “I stood in a corner, burst out crying, and I just couldn’t catch my breath. Police took it seriously, and through the stadium CCTV they were able to pinpoint him. There was a moment when they traced his steps coming into the ground, and it was harrowing to watch. He never took his eyes off me. He came in at the back of the stand and then, over a 20-minute period, moved down and stopped several times until he was about a metre away from me.”
 From there, the response was unusually swift by the standards of stalking cases. In the UK, only about six per cent of recorded offences end in a suspect being charged, while under two per cent ever result in a criminal conviction. Although Pike finds such figures “frightening”, she considers herself amongst the fortunate few. “That’s one of the reasons I wanted to speak out about this,” she explains. “The police immediately took it seriously. They arrested the guy the morning after the match, they came to my house to take my full statement, and they just went full steam ahead from there. I later found out that he had been messaging my best friend, her husband, plus other people I know. When police went through his devices, they found pictures of him sitting in the pub around the corner from my house. There were even photographs of my ex-husband’s car.”
 It is not the first stalking ordeal suffered by a high-profile female sports presenter in this country. Last year Laura Woods described to Telegraph Sport how she had been bombarded for three years by an obsessed female Liverpool fan, who would send her birthday cards that read: “Today’s the day you were born and tonight’s the night you’re going to die.” The woman was later jailed for 14 months. 
 For all that Pike has hesitated about sharing her own experience, she wants to lay bare the fear and isolation that stalkers can cause their victims. “In my head, I was minimising this as a way of trying to protect myself,” she says. “But we shouldn’t minimise these things. You have to make sure that people know this behaviour isn’t OK.”
 Although the realisation her stalker had been caught proved cathartic, his subsequent release on bail – with strict conditions not to go near her – coincided with perhaps the worst day of her life. “I asked my parents to come around so that I could fill them in on everything that was happening,” she recalls. “My mum has stage-four bowel cancer. And as I told her about the stalking, she collapsed. I scrambled an ambulance, and she ended up in hospital for five weeks. The stalking came on top of an incredibly difficult year for my family, magnifying the pressure and anxiety.”
 It came as a tonic that she soon obtained a stalking protection order against the man, which prohibited him from visiting her village, approaching any of her relatives or friends, or attending the Etihad. Manchester City took the extra precaution of banning him in any case. In the months that followed, Pike did everything she could to make herself difficult to trace, changing her car number plate, avoiding the local shops, and varying her routes home. She also derived support from the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, the UK’s leading authority on stalking and one that provides a national helpline.
 “One of the sad things about this is that it has really affected my enjoyment of going to the Etihad,” she says. “I’m a lifelong Manchester City fan, and it would always be my place of safety. I was there throughout my divorce, the pandemic, all the awful things that happen in life, and I could still be happy there. I feel like that has been taken away from me.”
 Her route into football broadcasting was, to put it mildly, unorthodox. In the early 2000s, Pike initially gained recognition at the peak of the lads’ mags era, winning FHM’s award as “High Street Honey of the Year”. It is a period that seems as though it belongs in a time capsule, especially given the recent testimony of Natalie Imbruglia, the Australian pop star, that she felt “exploited” and “traumatised” by a photoshoot for one such magazine. Pike, by contrast, insists that she felt no discomfort. “I very much look back on it with affection. Now and again, somebody will bring it up as a form of ‘gotcha’, but I’m not ashamed of it. I’m proud of it and it has brought me to where I am today.
 “Would I make those decisions now, as a 43-year-old mother? No, I wouldn’t. But I was 21. And I’m not going to allow anybody to make me feel shame for anything I’ve done in my career, then or now. That’s another reason why I want to tell my story, because it’s about showing that women are strong, that we won’t be stopped or discouraged.”
 It would be another decade before she cultivated her first opportunities in sport. “My only regret,” she says, “is that I didn’t have the self-belief to do it 20 years ago.” Having modelled the Manchester City kit for the 2008-09 campaign, the first of the Abu Dhabi-controlled era, she was eventually entrusted with being the club’s main in-house presenter, interviewing everybody from Guardiola to Liam Gallagher. She has covered every twist of the past 15 years’ transformation, now the subject of the fiercest scrutiny after the Premier League’s verdict last week that it was all achieved through artificially inflated commercial revenue. City employees are restricted from speaking about the case until the appeal is complete.
 Expanding her platform beyond City, Pike, who was born in Edinburgh, took a lead in broadcasting Scotland’s extraordinary takeover of Boston at this year’s World Cup. “I really needed this,” she said at the time, even if nobody knew the full reasons why it meant so much to her.
 Pike becomes tearful as she reflects on her Massachusetts summer, which provided a precious escape from the state of hyper-vigilance her stalker had forced her to adopt. “It makes me emotional thinking about it, because it came at the perfect time, and it was such a release from everything else that was happening,” she says. “It helps restore faith in human nature, I guess.”
 In a Manchester courtroom last Friday, she was finally able to close the book on an anguished episode, as the man who had hounded her received a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months. She had the option of asking for a screen to separate herself from the stalker, she declined, choosing instead to deliver her victim impact statement directly to him. “I did that as a means of taking back power in that situation,” she says. “I thought, ‘I don’t need to hide. I’ve got nothing to hide about’. Seeing him sentenced, and hearing the judge emphasise the seriousness of the case, I felt strong. And I felt an overwhelming relief that I could now get on with my life.”
 What happened to her has changed her profoundly, casting a shadow that has taken the best part of a year to lift. But she trusts that by telling people, she might help illuminate stalking’s true toll and the human scars that can lie beneath even the most ebullient personas on screen.”

Manchester City keep entertaining. Maresca is learning to love the chaos
Enzo Maresca summed up his feelings about Manchester City’s chaotic 5-3 victory over Sunderland in a way that many might expect. “To be honest, I prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3,” he smiled.
 Maresca arrived with a reputation for slow, methodical football. He threatened to walk out on Leicester City after fans groaned at his possession-based approach, despite his side being top of the Championship by 10 points in January 2024 — and many took Chelsea player Cole Palmer’s recent reference to ‘safe zones’ as an attack on the Italian’s preference for structure.
 Even sources close to City’s first team in recent years, familiar with Maresca’s style of play as an opposition manager, believed he was more suited to the City side that won the treble in 2022-23, rather than the more dynamic squad of players that they have assembled since.
 And while there is plenty for City to improve upon, having been given the runaround by Brian Brobbey and almost conceding a comedy own goal that would have made it 4-4 on Sunday, Maresca’s City side are looking like entertainers at this early stage — and that could be the theme of their season.

Andy Burnham, UK Prime Minister: "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up & "I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city" [BBC News]
Andy Burnham has said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.
 The prime minister said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and he praised the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister and royal family member - for investing in Manchester.
 An independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 charges they faced, a verdict that City are expected to appeal.
 The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.
 It comes as the Independent Football Regulator – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues".
 The regulator suggested it would be exploring options – including whether to strip the owners of their licence to own the club – once the disciplinary process was completed.
 Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.
 The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".
 The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment. City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving City and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty.
 The punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they had won in the affected period.
 Some fans and pundits have questioned how the club's owners can carry on if they deliberately breached rules over the course of nine years.
 Asked by the BBC's political editor Chris Mason if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burham said on Wednesday: "I would be really concerned to lose them.
 "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."
 Burnham, the mayor of Greater Manchester until June, added: "I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city".
 He said he was "of course" confident that his own interactions with City's owners when he was mayor would stand up to scrutiny.
 Burnham made his comments amid widespread shock in football about the scale of the independent commission's findings – and the strength of Premier League comments about City's actions.
 Burnham was speaking to the BBC from Hill Dickinson Stadium, the home of Everton, the team he supports.
 Everton had their own run in with Premier League financial rules when they were charged and deducted 10 points for more minor breaches in November 2023, reduced to six on appeal.
 Burnham said: "Everton was in this position a few years ago and you might remember that I fought for Everton in that situation because I still hold the view very firmly that they weren't fairly treated in that process."
 Drawing a comparison between that and City's current predicament, he added: "I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and with hindsight I think more people would say that wasn't fair, the way that was handled.
 "So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming prime minister."
 It is "frustrating when people rush to judgement", Burnham said.
 He accepted there was "a lot at stake" for City fans, the club and Manchester itself.
 But he added it would be wrong for him to intervene.
 City have said in a statement they are "both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission" and maintained their innocence of all the accusations made.
